name: typestate
intent: Encode an object's state in its type - a type parameter or a distinct state type - so that only the operations legal in the current state exist and every transition is a checked, type-changing step.
problem: An object's methods are valid only in certain states (a closed file cannot be read, a client that has not connected cannot send), but the state lives in a runtime field: callers must remember the protocol, illegal calls still compile and fail at run time, and the legal sequences are documented rather than enforced.
context: Statically typed languages with generics or usable distinct-type support, where a small, fixed set of states and legal transitions is known at compile time: protocol handshakes, resource lifecycles (files, sockets, peripherals), staged builders and configuration objects, and single-owner workflows. It pays where a wrong sequence is expensive - hardware, protocols, money - and the state machine is stable.
benefits: Illegal transitions disappear from the language instead of being caught at run time: calling an operation in the wrong state is a compile error, so the protocol needs no defensive checks and no tests for the impossible case.
The API itself documents the protocol: a parameter typed Handle<Connected> is machine-checked evidence that the connect step ran, which removes whole classes of 'you must call X first' preconditions.
Zero runtime cost where type parameters and zero-sized markers are erased: no state field, no branch and no allocation is added just to enforce the order.
Transitions that consume the old state also prevent stale-handle bugs: after use the previous value is invalid, not merely outdated.
Refactors are compiler-guided: changing the protocol turns every affected call site into a build error instead of leaving a silent runtime path.
State-specific operations live together with the state they belong to, which keeps large protocol implementations readable and stops invalid operations leaking onto the shared API.
tradeoffs: The state machine is frozen at compile time: transitions whose validity depends on runtime data cannot be encoded, so those states must be modelled as an enum plus branching, re-introducing runtime checks.
API surface multiplies with states and edges - one type, one implementation block and one method per legal transition - which is visible boilerplate for anything but a small protocol.

The consume half exists only where the language has move or linearity semantics; in C#, Java, TypeScript, Go, pre-5.9 Swift and C, copies or aliases of a state remain usable, so the guarantee degrades to 'the call is checked', not 'the old state is gone'.

Compile errors move to call sites and read as missing methods or unsatisfied constraints ('no method named send', 'cannot prove MissingPort =:= HasPort'), which can be harder to diagnose than a runtime guard with a message.

Typed handles resist erasure: storing several states in one collection, dynamic dispatch or FFI requires removing the state from the type, and the guarantee is lost exactly where it would have been useful.
Change cost is high: adding a state or an edge rewrites signatures, implementation blocks and tests across the codebase; the compiler finds them, but the diff is wide.
Correctness depends on discipline: casts, reflection, untyped callers or unsafe blocks can forge states, so typestate is a correctness tool, not a security boundary.
It demands type-system fluency (generics, marker types, ownership) from reviewers and newcomers, and opaque diagnostics slow teams that do not already know the pattern.

participants.responsibility: Marker type or state class representing one protocol state; it defines which transition operations exist and, in the class-per-state form, holds the data that is only meaningful in that state.
The handle whose type parameter (or concrete class) names the current state; it carries the data shared by all states and is the receiver of every operation.
A method or function that exists only for one source state, performs the step and returns the value typed with the destination state; in linear realizations it consumes the source value.
The single way to obtain the initial state - a constructor, factory function or associated new() - kept private or singular so callers cannot enter the protocol in the middle.
The enforcement mechanism: method resolution and type or bound checking decide at compile time whether the sequence written in the source is legal.
Code that walks the protocol; it cannot name intermediate states except through the transitions, so it cannot skip or repeat a step the protocol forbids.

use_cases: Staged builders where build() must not compile before every required property is supplied (typed request builders, configuration objects).
Resource lifecycles: files, sockets and streams whose read/write/close operations are meaningful only after open and before close.
Protocol handshakes - connect, authenticate, exchange, disconnect - including TLS or HTTP session setup and stateful client APIs.
Embedded peripheral configuration: a GPIO pin or timer whose mode (input, output, alternate function) is a type parameter, so wrong-mode register access is a compile error.
Transaction and workflow objects: begin, mutate, commit or roll back, where committing twice or mutating after commit must not be expressible.
Iterators and streams with an exhausted state, where next() consumes the iterator until it yields the end state.
Hardware or network state machines where a wrong sequence causes a fault rather than a catchable error (bus faults, half-open connections).

Embedded HALs in the Rust ecosystem (embedded-hal and device crates such as stm32f4xx-hal) model a pin as Pin<M> with its mode as the type parameter: set_high() compiles only for an output-mode pin and into_input()/into_output() consume the old pin, as prescribed by the Embedded Rust Book's GPIO design chapter.

The Checker Framework for Java runs typestate analysis over unmodified code: its Called Methods and Resource Leak checkers track @MustCall obligations so an InputStream cannot be read before its required initialization methods ran and must be closed on every path - the state is inferred by a checker rather than written into the type.

TypeScript builder libraries such as ts-fluent-builder thread a phantom state type through the builder's generics so build() only compiles once every required property is present, turning missing-field errors from runtime throws into compile errors.
avoid_when: The next legal transition depends on data only known at run time (user input, configuration bytes, database rows): use an enum state plus exhaustive branching, not types.
The state set is large and densely connected (most-to-most transitions): the type and method multiplication outweighs the safety; a transition table or statechart library is simpler.
The language has no generics or no static checking at all (plain JavaScript, Ruby, Python without a type checker, C without opaque-type discipline): use a runtime state machine with guards instead.
The state machine is small and local with one or two call sites: an assertion or a runtime guard is cheaper to read and maintain.
Different states carry substantially different data and the value must live in a homogeneous collection: an algebraic enum (sum type) with pattern matching is the natural tool.
The real concern is value validity rather than call order: validate at construction with smart constructors instead of encoding a sequence.
anti_patterns: Using type parameters as a substitute for value validation: the sequence of calls is checked, but the host name or the port may still be nonsense.

Forgetting linearity: transitions that take a shared reference, or return 'this' in a language with reference semantics, leave the old state usable and let invalid sequences through the type check that was supposed to stop them.
One marker type per combination of flags instead of per independent flag: the type space explodes combinatorially where Set/Unset slots would be linear.
Exposing constructors or public marker fields, which lets callers manufacture values in any state and nullifies the whole encoding.
Encoding a runtime-driven workflow as typestate and then casting or downcasting at the boundary to recover a variable state - the guarantee is erased exactly where it was needed.
Treating typestate as a security control: an attacker is not constrained by the type system of the code being attacked.
Rewriting a whole domain model as type-level state when only one call-order constraint matters; the ceremony then hides the one invariant that counts.
design_principles: Make illegal states unrepresentable: extend the functional-modelling idea from states to transitions, so an illegal sequence cannot be written at all.
Fail fast at the earliest possible moment: the type checker is the cheapest place to reject a protocol violation.
Encapsulation and information hiding: private constructors and private marker fields keep the state space closed and force callers through the transitions.
Single responsibility per state: each state type owns exactly the operations that are legal in it.
Explicit interfaces as documentation: a transition's type signature states its precondition and its effect on the state.
Design by contract: operations exist only where their preconditions hold, so an out-of-state call is impossible rather than an error path.
best_practices: Keep constructors and marker fields private or sealed, and expose exactly one way to reach the initial state.
Make transitions consume or replace the value and return the destination state; never leave the source state usable.

Parameterize per independent flag (Set/Unset, Connected/Disconnected) instead of enumerating combinations, and put shared operations on the generic implementation with state-specific ones on the state's own implementation.
Use zero-sized marker types with the language's phantom-data mechanism so the encoding erases at run time; do not store markers in fields.
Model runtime-decided states as an enum and branch explicitly; keep the typed form for sequences the compiler can see statically.
Prove the guarantee with compile-fail tests (documentation tests, guard-compilefail files) because a passing test suite cannot demonstrate that an illegal call is rejected.
Keep the shared payload in the protocol value and state-specific data in the state itself when the language allows it, rather than forcing every state to carry every field.
Name marker types after the protocol's states and confine their module scope to the API boundary so foreign states cannot be invented.
sources: Strom & Yemini, "Typestate: A Programming Language Concept for Enhancing Software Reliability", IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 12(1), 1986 - the originating description of typestate and typestate checking.
Aldrich, Sunshine, Saini & Sparks, "Typestate-Oriented Programming" (OOPSLA 2009) - states as first-class abstractions in the object model.
https://docs.rust-embedded.org/book/design-patterns/hal/gpio.html - the Embedded Rust Book's GPIO design chapter: pin mode and state encoded as typestate with consuming transitions.
https://docs.rs/stm32f4xx-hal/latest/stm32f4xx_hal/gpio/index.html - stm32f4xx-hal GPIO module: real pins whose operating mode is a type parameter.
https://checkerframework.org/manual/ - Checker Framework manual: the Called Methods and Resource Leak checkers implement typestate analysis over Java resources via @MustCall obligations.
https://github.com/NathanJAdams/fluent-builder - ts-fluent-builder: TypeScript builder whose phantom-type state makes an incomplete build() a compile error.
https://blog.yoshuawuyts.com/state-machines-3 - critique of type states: runtime-driven transitions are verbose to integrate and typed state leaks into the API.

https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3475061.3475082 - 'Retrofitting Typestates into Rust' (PEPM 2022): boilerplate, weak unaided guarantees and aliasing/concurrency pressure in hand-rolled typestate encodings.
